raw_response:
# Self-hosted remote access to Windows PCs without individual inbound firewall rules

The most direct fit is a remote-support system in which the Windows agent and the technician both connect outward to a server you operate. This removes the need to forward an incoming port to every target PC. It still requires installing or launching an agent, permitting its outbound traffic, and making the central server reachable. The ranked options below distinguish finished remote-access tools from a component-based alternative.

## 1. Remote Utilities with your own RU Server

**URL:** https://www.remoteutilities.com/product/self-hosted-server.php

RU Server is the strongest verified match: its Internet-ID relay accepts outbound connections from both the Windows Host and the technician's Viewer, bringing the connection through your own server. The product page explicitly describes this connection direction and the absence of endpoint port forwarding. Its port documentation distinguishes Internet-ID operation from direct connections, which would require an inbound Host port. Use the self-hosted Internet-ID configuration for this requirement.

The remaining endpoint work is deploying the Host, configuring its server and access credentials, and ensuring outbound traffic is permitted. A reachable central Windows server and appropriate product licensing are still required.

**Date evidence:** A vendor article dated November 27, 2016 explicitly describes Hosts connecting to either a public or a self-hosted relay, establishing the core arrangement before the December 4, 2016 cutoff. Current licensing and current features should not be assumed to describe the 2016 release.

Sources: https://www.remoteutilities.com/blog/version-65-online-statuses-in-viewer-address-book/ and https://www.remoteutilities.com/support/docs/ports-used-by-remote-utilities/?hide_main_note=2990

## 2. UltraVNC with a self-hosted Repeater and reverse connections

**URL:** https://uvnc.com/downloads/ultravnc-repeater/83-ultravnc-repeater.html

UltraVNC's Repeater provides the central relay mechanism: the Windows VNC server initiates a connection to the repeater, and a viewer joins the corresponding connection. The official guide shows a Windows service configured to reconnect to the repeater using an identifier. This is useful when the endpoints sit behind NAT and you control a publicly reachable relay.

This requires more configuration than a complete remote-support portal: distribute the VNC service configuration and unique identifiers, configure the central repeater, and enable authentication and encryption. An identifier alone is not adequate access protection. The inspected public source also defines connection, reconnect and repeater command-line switches.

**Date evidence:** The live download page contains 2026 updates. The guide has a 2016-looking generated key filename, and the current source contains a 2009 comment, but neither establishes the publication date of the inspected material. I therefore leave the candidate's historical evidence status unknown.

Sources: https://www.uvnc.eu/download/1210/Repeater.pdf and https://github.com/ultravnc/UltraVNC/blob/main/winvnc/winvnc/winvnc.h

## 3. SimpleHelp

**URL:** https://simple-help.com/self-hosted-remote-access

SimpleHelp is a packaged self-hosted option covering attended support and unattended access. Its documentation describes remote services connecting outward to the SimpleHelp server, avoiding inbound ports on the managed machines; the self-hosting page identifies the server as infrastructure controlled by the operator.

This is appropriate when you want a central support workflow rather than assembling a relay and viewer yourself. You must deploy its remote-access service to the target machines, operate a reachable server, and arrange the relevant commercial licence. Blocking outbound traffic can still prevent a connection.

**Date evidence:** The inspected product pages are live and undated, so their availability and precise capabilities at the 2016 cutoff remain unverified. An older vendor demonstration appeared in search results, but its page could not be fetched; I do not treat that failed open as verified historical evidence.

Supporting source: https://simple-help.com/headless-server-remote-access

## 4. Reverse SSH forwarding with Bitvise SSH Client, plus RDP or VNC

**URL:** https://bitvise.com/port-forwarding

A plausible alternative is to make each Windows PC establish an SSH connection to your central server, then use server-to-client forwarding to reach the PC's local RDP or VNC service. Bitvise documents server-to-client forwarding, including that its destination address is interpreted on the SSH-client side. Applying that mechanism to a local desktop service is an architectural inference, not an inspected turnkey deployment.

This avoids a public inbound connection to each PC, but adds tunnel configuration, per-machine port mapping, credentials and reconnection management. RDP must already be enabled and supported by the Windows edition; VNC needs its own server. The SSH client and local desktop service must be allowed to communicate.

**Date evidence:** The inspected Bitvise documentation is live and undated; this run did not verify a dated version available by the cutoff.

Supporting sources: https://bitvise.com/tunnelier and https://bitvise.com/remote-desktop

## Evidence limits

These are documented fits and a proposed composition, not claims that I deployed or tested them. Remote Utilities has direct dated evidence before the cutoff; the other candidates remain explicitly undated. The unauthenticated grep.app attempt failed, so the code evidence came through a public web search indexing GitHub and subsequent source-page inspection, not successful native code search. Discovery used nine search queries and sixteen opened-document attempts, including failures and a second source-page read; three queries and four opens remain for the separate checks.
